highlight.title: Desk Review: Recent Methodologies on AI and Labour
highlight.summary: This toolkit synthesises recent methodologies for analysing AI's effects on employment, wages, and productivity, highlighting a critical shift from occupation-level to task-level analysis that better captures heterogeneity within jobs. The review underscores that task-based frameworks reveal more nuanced displacement dynamics than traditional occupational classifications. (Papagiannaki & Geisler, Zenodo, 2026-03-06)

highlight.title: Enhancing BLS Methodologies for Projecting AI's Impact on Employment
highlight.summary: This policy paper proposes comprehensive enhancements to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics forecasting methods, arguing that traditional extrapolation techniques are inadequate for capturing AI-driven labor market transformation. The authors present a data-driven framework for measuring occupational exposure and displacement risk across sectors. (Joshi, Preprints, 2026-03-06)

highlight.title: AI and the Future of Work: Occupational Status Perceptions Among University Students
highlight.summary: A survey of university students finds that AI is reshaping perceptions of occupational social status, with students re-evaluating the prestige and long-term viability of various careers in light of automation risk. The study highlights that entry-level and routine white-collar roles are perceived as most vulnerable, influencing students' career alignment decisions. (Liu et al., Behavioral Sciences, 2026-03-04)

highlight.title: Digital Technology Facilitates Union Busting: Surveillance and Worker Suppression
highlight.summary: This study documents how employers leverage digital technologies—including AI-powered surveillance and automated scheduling—to counter union organizing efforts, erecting new barriers to collective bargaining in the United States. The findings suggest algorithmic management tools are increasingly deployed as instruments of labor control, with downstream effects on worker wages and conditions. (Reiber et al., arXiv, 2026-03-03)

highlight.title: Capability Thresholds in Embodied Intelligence Trigger Phase Transitions in Manufacturing Geography
highlight.summary: This paper argues that advances in embodied AI and robotics represent a paradigm-level disruption to manufacturing topology not seen since Ford's assembly line, with capability thresholds triggering abrupt geographic and structural shifts in production. The analysis implies significant displacement of manufacturing-adjacent white-collar and operational roles as intelligent automation matures. (Fang, Tao & Li, arXiv, 2026-03-03)
